title: Paralyzed Veterans of America v. D.C. Arena L.P.
lead: Wheelchair users challenged an arena’s views during moments when spectators stood. The owners attacked a technical manual’s legal force, while the users sought complete compliance rather than the district court’s substantial-compliance remedy.

actors.name: D.C. Arena owners
actors.role: Developers of the proposed downtown Washington MCI Center; appealed standing-spectator sightline requirements.

actors.name: Paralyzed Veterans of America and individual wheelchair users
actors.role: Private ADA plaintiffs and cross-appellants seeking universal wheelchair-seat coverage.

actors.name: Department of Justice
actors.role: DOJ; promulgated accessibility standards and guidance, participated only as amicus.

actors.name: Access Board
actors.role: Drafted the underlying guideline but supplied an explanation DOJ did not expressly adopt.

proceedings: District court found integration adequate and dispersal inadequate; only sightlines went to appeal.
Court accepted DOJ’s interpretation but approved revised plans with substantial rather than universal standing-spectator views.
D.C. Circuit affirmed both appeal and cross-appeal without separate opinions.
limits: The 1997 interpretation-change doctrine was later rejected by Perez in 2015. This historical holding separately classified the guidance as interpretive and sustained a private equitable remedy; it did not establish every arena requirement or a universal one-hundred-percent rule.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The accessibility agencies address comparable views without matching explanations
sections.cue: Which statements came from the Board and which from DOJ?
paragraphs: The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) prohibited disability discrimination in public accommodations and required covered new facilities to be accessible and usable. Congress assigned the Department of Justice (DOJ) standards and rulemaking. Standard 4.33.3 required integrated wheelchair areas, admission-price choice, comparable sightlines, companion seats, and multiple wheelchair locations for facilities above 300 seats.

The Access Board drafted the underlying guideline. Its January 1991 proposal recognized that generic sightline language might not solve obstruction when spectators stand and requested comments. DOJ proposed adopting the Board’s standards and directed comments there. In July the Board retained general wording while saying later recreation guidelines would address standing spectators. DOJ issued identical language the same day but did not adopt that explanation.

A midlevel DOJ official told stadium operators in a 1992 speech that standing-spectator views were unnecessary. By mid-1993, DOJ took the contrary position in Olympic-venue investigations. In December 1994 it published a technical-manual supplement without notice and comment expressly requiring views over spectators expected to stand. The legal significance and authority of these different statements became disputed.

sources.pinpoint: Framework and agency chronology; 117 F.3d at 580–82, 586–87

sections.title: The arena selects plans with only some unobstructed wheelchair views
sections.cue: What relief did the private plaintiffs obtain below?
paragraphs: The owners planned the downtown Washington MCI Center for basketball, hockey, concerts, and other events, where excitement would foreseeably cause spectators to stand. A month after the manual supplement, they selected four seating configurations: basketball, hockey, and two concert arrangements. Wheelchair seating exceeded one percent of capacity and spanned prices and locations, but only some places provided views over standing spectators. The owners admitted knowing DOJ’s interpretation when selecting them.

Paralyzed Veterans and individual wheelchair users sued privately, contesting integration, dispersal, and sightlines. DOJ declined repeated invitations to intervene, appeared as amicus, and was denied a second amicus submission. The district judge found adequate integration and inadequate dispersal; only sightlines were appealed.

The judge accepted DOJ’s interpretation but permitted substantial compliance given uneven agency enforcement, competing practical requirements, and owners’ good faith. Revised plans provided standing-spectator views at 78 percent of wheelchair locations in one configuration and 85–88 percent in the others. A later opinion summary used 75–88 percent; the specific configuration figures describe the approved plans here.

sources.pinpoint: Arena and district court; 117 F.3d at 581–82 & n.1, 588

sections.title: Silberman finds the wording broad enough to include standing spectators
sections.cue: Why did the private lawsuit and Board drafting not defeat deference?
paragraphs: The owners argued that comparable sightlines addressed distribution alone, alternatively sought independent judicial interpretation, and claimed an unauthorized new or changed substantive rule. They did not argue conflict with the ADA itself. Judge Silberman, writing with Chief Judge Edwards and Judge Sentelle, noted that other words separately addressed dispersal and price. An unobstructed view naturally supplied additional content. Earlier private standards established no settled exclusion of temporary obstruction, though ambiguity remained between standing people and permanent structures.

Applying 1997 deference precedents, the panel sustained a permissible agency interpretation unless plainly erroneous or inconsistent. It acknowledged incentives for vague rules but treated APA procedure as a constraint against publishing empty generalities and adding the actual law later. This standard contained real substantive content and alerted readers to possible protection against standing spectators. The panel distinguished procedural limits from constitutional nondelegation and considered beneficiaries’ interests as well as regulated parties’ reliance.

DOJ’s statutory administrative responsibility, not special insight into drafting, supported deference after adopting the Board’s language. It had rulemaking duties and a congressional mandate for technical manuals despite lacking administrative adjudication and enforcing through courts. That role differed from a mere prosecutor or the cited divided-agency settings. A private action did not erase it.

sources.pinpoint: Text and historical deference; 117 F.3d at 582–85 & nn.2–5

sections.title: No authoritative earlier DOJ interpretation had been established
sections.cue: How did the panel separately classify the manual?
paragraphs: The panel stated that fundamentally changing a definitive regulatory interpretation required notice and comment, unlike then-recognized flexibility to revise statutory interpretations under Chevron. Even under that doctrine, owners failed to show a qualifying earlier DOJ position. The Board’s deferral was not necessarily DOJ’s view, and DOJ could exceed Board minimums. A midlevel speech and later testimony about earlier intentions were not authoritative departmental judgments. Owners also knew the manual before choosing plans, defeating their claimed detrimental reliance.

Independently, the court examined whether the manual itself was legislative. Labels and agency intentions did not control. Guidance explaining a duty fairly included in an existing regulation differed from a requirement with independent force of law. Practical consequences alone did not make it legislative. Close textual connection supported interpretive status, whereas supplying real substance to an empty norm pointed the other way.

Comparable sightlines already supplied an arguable enforcement basis. The standing-spectator explanation was not sufficiently distinct or additive to demand notice and comment. This classification rationale remained separate from the panel’s interpretation-change doctrine, later rejected by the Supreme Court.

sources.pinpoint: Change and classification; 117 F.3d at 586–88 & n.6

sections.title: The users’ cross-appeal cannot turn the manual into a universal command
sections.cue: Why did the judge retain remedial discretion?
paragraphs: Plaintiffs sought one-hundred-percent compliance as an asserted DOJ requirement, but the manual did not state that position. Other agency materials and the Olympic settlement referred to all or substantially all locations. Improved views from higher positions or section boundaries could also conflict with integration, making practical tradeoffs relevant.

Plaintiffs said the rejected second DOJ brief would limit exceptions to structural impracticality, technical infeasibility, or comparable obstruction for standing patrons. The panel questioned deference to that litigation refinement but independently upheld discretion to reject the additional brief. DOJ had repeatedly declined intervention.

This was private equitable litigation, not direct review of an agency order. The district judge could shape relief within the regulation’s and manual’s latitude, and an appellate amicus filing did not enlarge the plaintiffs’ entitlement. DOJ could clarify its manual if it wanted uniformity.

sources.pinpoint: Cross-appeal and remedy; 117 F.3d at 588–89 & n.7

sections.title: Both sides lose their appeals, with later law limiting one rationale
paragraphs: The D.C. Circuit affirmed the district judgment on appeal and cross-appeal. Owners remained obliged to provide substantial standing-spectator sightlines, and plaintiffs did not obtain coverage at every wheelchair location. There was no separate concurrence or dissent. The judgment approved these equitable arrangements rather than conclusively specifying all ADA arena duties.

In 2015, Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Association rejected requiring notice and comment merely because an agency significantly changes a genuinely interpretive rule, while leaving the interpretive-versus-legislative distinction intact. That later holding limits use of the 1997 change doctrine; it was not the doctrine applied by this panel when resolving the MCI Center dispute.

sources.pinpoint: Result and later treatment; 117 F.3d at 589; source brief’s Perez discussion, 575 U.S. at 96–97, 100–07
